detail: While planning V0, nearly committed to building the automated retro loop (v1) before dogfooding it by hand on a real project — build ahead of validation. Corrected: Wizard-of-Oz the loop manually first, then automate only if it produces value.

On the Two Way Invoice Sync dogfood, init.md's emitter (phase 4) wrote CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md with byte-identical content (confirmed via diff -q). Duplication violates token-economy T1, and Claude Code reads ONLY CLAUDE.md while AGENTS.md is the cross-vendor standard. Fixed: AGENTS.md canonical + CLAUDE.md = one-line @AGENTS.md import.

Built the strict-path-guard hook using permissionDecision 'defer' from an unverified claude-code-guide answer. 'defer' is headless-only and wrong for an interactive passive warning (correct: exit 0 + additionalContext, no permissionDecision). Caught by the crossed adversarial review + a grounding pass. Lesson: ground every API claim against the docs before shipping code — even a claim from a sub-agent. voice V2 (verify before asserting) applies to sub-agent output too.

The build plan specified `claude -p --output-format stream-json` for the llm/ adapter without ever running it. Live probing found three errors: stream-json errors without --verbose; a naive invocation inherits the caller's whole ambient config (MCP servers, plugins, SessionStart hooks) costing 140,682 input tokens / $0.84 for a one-word answer versus ~11.4k / $0.03-0.08 hermetic — a 10x cost gap that would have silently destroyed the frugality thesis; and --bare, the obvious fix, forces ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and never reads OAuth, which would lose the subscription cost advantage. Validating risk #1 at Step 0 instead of at integration time was correct. Same class as sig-0003.

Using --system-prompt (replacing rather than appending) made the model leak raw tool-call markup (</parameter>, </invoke>) INTO a schema-valid string field. Native --json-schema validation passed on a payload that was unusable. Empirical proof that the LLM verdict contract needs contamination detection plus validate-and-retry, not just schema validation — the design assumed schema validation would be sufficient. Fixed in core/llm/verdict.ts with the real payload as a regression fixture; --append-system-prompt is now mandatory.

The first contamination check matched a bare ' is unclosed') and turned every front-end review into a retry loop that fails closed. Caught by writing the false-positive test before trusting the guard. Lesson: a guard against garbage needs a test proving it accepts the legitimate case, not only that it rejects the bad one.

ADR-0008's pre-registered kill criterion was measured at Step 0: a correctness lens returned 10/10 correct and unanimous on BOTH a known-good and a known-bad fixture (claude 2.1.225, sonnet, $0.79 for 20 calls). The agent-lens-can-earn-block assumption survives its first test. CAVEAT, recorded so it is not overclaimed: the fixtures are mirror-image and unambiguous (removing vs adding a null check before a dereference). This proves the harness works and the easy case is stable; it does NOT prove stability on borderline diffs, which is where a gate actually lives. Harder fixtures are owed before any lens ships as severity: block.

sig-0005's contamination rule rejected ANY tool-call markup in a verdict. Measured over 80 calibration runs, the artifact is a well-formed TRAILING suffix (the model closes its tool call inside the string) with complete, correct prose in front of it — and it is size-correlated: 0/40 runs on diffs under 10 lines, 13/40 on 11-15 line diffs. Rejecting the whole verdict discarded CORRECT answers and burned 3 billed retries into the same deterministic failure, leaving the gate blind on ~33% of realistic-length diffs. Fixed: strip the trailing artifact and report it via `sanitized`; markup embedded mid-content still fails closed. Re-measured live: 0/8 blind, down from 33%. Lesson: a guard written from a 2-sample observation was calibrated to the wrong failure shape — the rule was right in kind and wrong in degree.

`.sdd/architecture.md` recorded '--append-system-prompt clean 2/2' as evidence the contamination was fixed. That was 2 runs on a one-line prompt. At realistic diff lengths the same contamination recurs on a third of calls (sig-0008). The claim was not wrong so much as measured on an input unlike the real workload. Lesson: an evidence table is only as good as the representativeness of its inputs — record N and the input size next to any stability claim, not just the ratio.

`npm run calibrate -- --filter race` printed 'PASS — this lens may be declared severity: block' after measuring only 2 of 10 fixtures. A subset run that emits the global promotion verdict is how a lens gets promoted on the fixtures it happens to be good at — the precise result-fitting ADR-0008 pre-registers against. Fixed: a filtered run now prints PARTIAL and states it cannot promote. Lesson: any tool that can run on a subset must say so in its verdict, not only in its invocation.

Changing an agent-lens prompt from 'does this introduce a bug?' to 'name a concrete failing input under the change's stated contract, else pass' removed nearly all false positives (nullish-good 8/10 -> 5/5, boundary-good 7/10 -> 5/5) WITHOUT introducing false negatives (all five known-bad fixtures stayed 5/5). The obvious risk of raising the burden of proof for `fail` — starting to miss real bugs — did not materialise at N=5. Lesson: a flaky agent-lens is often a badly-specified one, not an unstable one; rewrite the lens before concluding the check cannot be calibrated. Still FAILS the bar: race-good flips 1/5.

scripts/calibrate.ts kept its own copy of the review lens with a comment saying 'must stay in sync with .sdd/checks/correctness.md'. That is a receipt-integrity hole: on drift you calibrate one prompt and ship another, and the check's recorded `calibration:` block vouches for text that never ran — a receipt that certifies the wrong artifact. Fixed: the harness now loads the lens through the check registry. Lesson: anything that produces a RECEIPT must read the artifact it certifies, never a copy of it. Same class as ADR-0006's warning that a version string is not identity.

A deterministic check runs through a shell, so a MISSING BINARY is not a spawn error — the shell starts fine and exits 127. Read naively that is a non-zero exit, i.e. a failing check, so one missing tool would have BLOCKED every change in the repo and blamed the change for it. The gate lane found this by running the gate on this repo and now maps 126/127 to `errored`, checked BEFORE the exit code because a broken run usually also reports non-zero. Verified with npm and claude off PATH: two block-severity checks fully broken, verdict pass, blocking empty, exit 2. Lesson: 'the tool failed' and 'the code failed' arrive on the same channel (exit status) and must be separated deliberately, or a gate blames the author for its own breakage.

While verifying the gate blocks on a real failure, the mutation I applied was a NO-OP: I pattern-matched `status: "renamed"` but the source has `status: letter === "R" ? "renamed" : "copied"`, so perl replaced nothing. The gate correctly returned pass, and I nearly recorded that as 'the gate fails to block'. Caught by checking whether the mutation actually landed AND whether the tests actually went red before trusting the gate's answer. Lesson: a negative test must first prove it broke what it claims to have broken — otherwise you are measuring your own patch, not the system.

The first `wst run` gated with --range HEAD, which means working-tree-vs-HEAD. The crewmate COMMITS its work, so by gate time the working tree is clean and the diff is EMPTY: the gate matched no files, applied no checks, and correctly reported 'nothing about this change was verified' — while `wst run` printed PASSED above it. The gate's honesty is the only reason this was caught; a gate that reported a bare 'pass' for an empty diff would have hidden it. Fixed: capture the base commit before dispatch and gate `base..HEAD`, plus refuse outright when the crewmate committed nothing. Lesson: 'no checks ran' and 'all checks passed' are different results and must never share a success message.

Diagnosing the above, I inspected the worktree AFTER the run had already released it. `treehouse return --force` resets the worktree to the pool base, so the tree I examined had no src/ and no package.json — and I announced the bug was 'far worse', that the crewmate had branched from the wrong commit and worked on an empty tree. Wrong: the branch ref survived, and it held exactly the right four-file commit. The evidence I was reading was destroyed by the cleanup I had just run. Lesson: when a run cleans up after itself, diagnose from the artifacts that SURVIVE cleanup (branch refs, logs) — and state which state you are looking at before drawing a conclusion from it.

The first real `wst retro` returned 3 of 4 proposals as the literal word 'placeholder', one explaining 'I don't have visibility into .sdd/skills/voice.md'. Cause: the proposer runs HERMETIC (no tools, no filesystem, by design — it is a judge), so it was asked to amend a rule whose text it had never been shown. Fixed by putting the target skill's current content and the list of real skills into the prompt; the second run produced 5 substantive proposals citing real signals. Lesson: a hermetic judge can only reason about what is IN the prompt — every artifact it must judge has to be passed in, and 'it has tools' is a property of crewmates, not of judges.

The anti-poisoning gate checked that a rationale was non-EMPTY but not that it was substantive, so proposals whose entire body was 'placeholder' passed validation and reached the human. The model had honestly signalled it could not do the job and the gate treated that as a valid proposal. Fixed: reject placeholder/TBD markers and rationales under 60 chars. Lesson: a validator that only checks for absence will forward a non-answer — 'the model said something' is not the same as 'the model answered'.

Porting docs/woz/init.md to code surfaced that the WoZ SPEC ITSELF violates ADR-0004: its AGENTS.md template tells a bootstrapped repo to 'run the retro (see retro.md)' — a Whetstone document that does not exist in the target, so the reference dangles the moment the payload travels. Same bug class as the skills/recording.md citation fixed earlier, but this one was in the procedure rather than in an artifact, so every repo the procedure bootstrapped would have inherited it. The init lane described the retro inline instead. Lesson: a self-containment rule has to be enforced against the GENERATOR, not only audited on its output — the init code now runs a reference-closure check that refuses to emit a plan mentioning a path the plan does not create.

package.json had `files: ["dist"]`, so `.sdd/skills/` — the payload init copies into a target — was never published. Fixing that exposed a worse bug in findPayloadRoot(): it walked up from the module unbounded, so installed at <target>/node_modules/whetstone/dist/commands/ it would escape the package and find <target>/.sdd/skills — THE TARGET'S OWN SKILLS. init would copy a project's skills back onto itself and report success, indistinguishable from a correct bootstrap. Fixed: the walk stops at the package.json declaring name===whetstone and never crosses a node_modules boundary. Verified from a simulated install with a planted impostor skill. Lesson: a 'walk up until you find X' lookup has no notion of ownership — in a package that ships inside someone else's tree it will happily find THEIR X.

Verifying the payload-boundary fix, the test reported 'impostor survived' three times running — and all three were the HARNESS failing, not the code: first the simulated install lacked node_modules so the CLI died with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, then it died again on the same cause, then on an invalid --risk flag I had passed myself. Each time the impostor file was untouched simply because init never executed, which looks identical to init running and picking the wrong payload. Caught by asserting the mechanism RAN (wst.yaml exists) before reading the result — which is exactly xreview XR5 as amended by retro-0016, applied within the hour of writing it. Lesson: a negative result from a harness that never executed is not a result; assert execution before interpreting outcome.

The claude CLI exits NON-ZERO on its own terminal errors (notably error_max_budget_usd) while still writing a complete parseable envelope to stdout. execFile rejects on that exit code, and shell/claude.ts discarded stdout on rejection, so every budget exhaustion surfaced as kind 'spawn' (could not run the check) instead of 'budget' (ran out of money). classifyHardError already had a budget branch; it was simply unreachable on this path. The gate works hard to keep 'the tool broke' separate from 'the check failed', and the distinction was being destroyed one layer below it. Fixed: parse stdout on rejection when it is a complete envelope, rethrow only when it is not. Lesson: an adapter that drops output on a non-zero exit silently downgrades every structured error the tool took the trouble to report.

The correctness lens is systematically not running on realistic strict-tier changes. route() sends strict to opus, and the gate sends ONE call containing the entire matched diff under a fixed 0.50 USD ceiling. Measured on a real 114 KB diff: the call cost 0.607 USD and was killed by the cap, so the lens errored. Consequence lands on Layer 5: every strict PR renders NOT VERIFIED: correctness could not run. The gate is honest about it, which is why it was visible at all, but the differentiator is inert in practice. Candidate fixes: per-file or chunked lens calls, a tier-scaled budget, or both. Not yet fixed.

I claimed the 549-test suite was inflated by crewmates optimising for thoroughness, and proposed cutting tests in the lane-written annotate/ and checks/ files. Mutation testing refuted it. Score 34/40 (85%) killed; the 9.2-tests-per-mutation figure I called redundancy is mostly CROSS-FILE integration coupling, which is legitimate: a mutation in findings.ts kills tests in annotate.test.ts and body.test.ts because those exercise the pipeline. Reading the two largest crewmate files found no duplication either — 34 distinct behaviours in body.test.ts, 16 distinct properties in criticality.test.ts. Nothing was deleted. What the measurement DID produce was two real gaps (a block/advisory filter flip and a truncation off-by-one) that survived the whole suite, now closed and verified to kill their mutants. Lesson: 'this feels like too many tests' is a hypothesis, and mutation testing is cheap enough to test it before acting on it — the instrument found gaps, not bloat.

To prove the new pre-push hook blocks a bad push, I broke a test, ran `git add -A && git commit` and pushed. The commit swept up the hook, the CI workflow, the --no-lens flag and the status changes ALONGSIDE the deliberate sabotage. Undoing the sabotage with `git reset --hard HEAD~1` therefore destroyed all of it: four files gone from the working tree, test count 568 -> 566. Recovered via `git checkout <reflog-sha> -- <paths>`, verified the sabotage did NOT come back with it. Root cause: `git add -A` while the working tree contained both real work and a deliberate defect, then treating the commit as if it held only the defect. Lesson: never stage a deliberate defect with `-A`. Commit the real work FIRST, then make the defect as a separate uncommitted change so undoing it is `git checkout -- <file>` and cannot reach anything else.

The first thing automatic signal emission did was record my own deliberate sabotage as genuine friction. Proving the gate blocks requires breaking something on purpose, and the engine cannot distinguish a planted defect from a real one, so the evidence log gained a fabricated entry the moment it started writing itself. Removed by hand, and --no-emit is now reachable from the CLI so verifying the gate cannot pollute the record it produces. Note the shape: this is the same failure as sig-0025 (a negative control contaminating real work) one layer up, now in the evidence rather than the working tree. Lesson: any mechanism that records what it observes needs an explicit off switch for the runs where you are testing the mechanism itself, or its first act is to poison its own input.

`wst gate` routed from `provisionalRouting`, a stub that hard-coded `strict` and never read `.sdd/triage.yaml`. Its justifying comment said `core/triage/` "is being built in a parallel lane and does not exist yet" — but triage SHIPPED in the same PR, and `wst pr` was already consuming it (classify + route, pr.ts:219). So the gate, which IS the enforcement channel (pre-push hook + CI), ignored the project's own triage rules, while the annotation that describes the gate used them. Two commands could route the same change differently. Measured after the fix on its own diff: classified `light` selects [test, typecheck]; the old forced `strict` also selected `correctness`, the agent-lens — so until now every full gate run billed a model even on doc-only changes. It failed SAFE (over-verified), which is exactly why nobody noticed for a whole PR. Fixed by lifting `loadRules` out of pr.ts into `shell/sdd.ts` as `loadTriageRules` and calling classify+route in gate.ts. Note the shape: this is the SAME failure as the duplicated check runner (gate.ts:169) — a second implementation of a routing decision living in a composition root, which `.sdd/triage.yaml`'s own rule for `src/commands/**` predicts verbatim: "a decision found here is a design bug before it is a testing one". Lesson: a stub's justification is a claim with an expiry date. When the thing it stands in for lands, the comment becomes a lie that reads like documentation, and nothing in the toolchain checks it. Found by a human-guided read of the PR, NOT by the gate — the gate cannot catch this class.

The receipt input hash covered the changed files plus the check's declared `version`, and nothing else. `version` is hand-maintained and nothing in the schema forces a bump, so editing a check's `command` (npm test -> npm test -- --shard=1/4) left every existing receipt matching: the gate would report PASS for a check that had never run in its current form. Found by an external comparison against Trunk Check, which solves this with `affects_cache`. Note the asymmetry that makes it worse than the same bug elsewhere: a stale key in Turborepo replays an old build, a stale key here reports a clean gate on code no check examined. Fixed by hashing the behaviour-determining fields directly (command, review_lens) via a `CheckIdentity` built in ONE place (`identityOf` in gate/run.ts), so the hash the gate compares and the hash recordPass mints cannot diverge. RECEIPT_INPUT_FORMAT bumped 1 -> 2, so every receipt on disk is re-earned. Version SURVIVES as the manual override for behaviour changes the fields cannot observe. STILL OPEN and documented in place rather than hidden: the hash cannot see what the command reaches at runtime (.eslintrc, tsconfig, a pinned tool version, fixtures, env). The complete fix is an explicit `affects` path list in the check schema, which is a schema change and therefore a conversation. Lesson: a cache key must cover everything the cached claim depends on, and 'we version it by hand' is a promise, not a mechanism. Prefer hashing the thing over hashing a human's assertion about the thing.

`wst init`'s only overwrite guard covered `.sdd/`, but the plan writes AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json and .claude/hooks/ too, and `writePlan` is mkdir -p + writeFile with NO existence check. So a repo that had never seen Whetstone but did have hand-written versions of those four lost all of them, silently, no backup, not even a line in the output. CLAUDE.md is replaced by a ONE LINE pointer; .claude/settings.json by an object containing only Whetstone's hook, wiping permissions/env/statusLine/other hooks. Worst possible shape for a destructive bug: it fires on the FIRST command a new user runs, on the repo they are evaluating the tool with, and it takes exactly the files a careful team hand-maintains. The docstring also claimed `--force` 'prints what it is about to overwrite' and it did not, so the file asserted a safety property it did not have. Fixed with a pure `collisionsIn` over every planned path (files AND copies -- guarding only `files` would have left the whole skills payload open), each collision carrying a STAKE in the human's terms, because a bare path list does not distinguish an empty signals.jsonl coming back empty from losing a hand-written CLAUDE.md. --force now genuinely prints the list first. Verified end to end against a throwaway repo in the scratchpad, NOT this one (sig-0025/0026). Lesson: a guard's scope must be derived from what the operation writes, not from the one path that felt important when it was written. When the writer has no check of its own, the guard is the only thing between the plan and somebody's work -- so it belongs next to the plan, covering all of it.

`wst status` modelled hooks as one boolean, `hooksInstalled`, computed IN THE COMMAND as `hooksPath === '.githooks'`. git has exactly one core.hooksPath, so husky, lefthook and Whetstone are mutually exclusive — but the boolean could not tell 'nothing configured' from 'another tool configured', so a repo on `.husky` reported identically to a repo with no hooks and got told to run `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`. Following that disarms husky. Worse in combination with the fact that `wst init` never writes a `.githooks/` directory into a target repo: the advice would disarm the existing hooks AND install nothing in their place. Fixed by replacing the boolean with `HookFacts { configuredPath, whetstoneHooksPresent }` and branching three ways: another owner -> name it and give NO command, because choosing to disarm someone's setup is not status's call; no .githooks/ to point at -> say so; otherwise -> the original advice. The render names the owner too, since a bare 'NOT active' reads as 'nothing guards this repo', the opposite of the truth on a husky repo. Note WHERE the bug lived: the comparison was made in `src/commands/status.ts`, a composition root, which is exactly what `.sdd/triage.yaml`'s rule for `src/commands/**` warns about — 'a decision found here is a design bug before it is a testing one'. That is the THIRD finding this session with that shape (sig-0027, the duplicated check runner, and now this). Lesson: a boolean that answers 'is it ours?' hides 'whose is it?', and any advice derived from it will eventually be advice to overwrite a stranger's work. Model the owner, not the ownership.

FIRST SIGNAL EARNED FROM A LIVE RUN RATHER THAN WRITTEN BY HAND. `wst init --propose` shipped passing 16 unit tests and a prompt carrying the file list, scripts, commit subjects and detection evidence. The first real invocation returned a refusal: 'I cannot determine what this project is for from the evidence provided', and then named exactly what was missing — 'I was not shown the contents of package.json (no dependency list) or src/a.ts, which are the two things most likely to settle purpose'. The evidence-over-assertion rule worked (it refused to guess, and flagged zero risk because it could justify none), but the prompt was starving it. Nothing in the test suite could have caught this: every test asserted what the prompt CONTAINS, and the defect was what it OMITS. Fixed by inlining the README (truncated at 4000 chars) and the dependency NAMES (not versions — the pin is noise). Re-run on the same repo went from a refusal to three risk flags, each citing files, and one carrying its own falsification condition: 'INFERRED from dependencies only ... should be dropped if the bot uses long polling instead of a webhook'. Cost $0.16 -> $0.12, so more context was also cheaper than a refusal plus a retry. Also corrected a claim in the CLI hint that the call costs 'a few cents'; measured at ~$0.15. Lesson: for a hermetic judge, the prompt IS the world. Unit tests can pin what you put in it and can never tell you what you left out — only a live run can, and the model will usually say so if the prompt gives it permission to admit ignorance.

OBSERVED IN THE WILD, not constructed. A real `wst run` dispatch on the VPS produced the branch `run/fix-init-see-monorepos-and-their-tests-i`, where the trailing `-i` is the amputated start of `inside`. `branchNameFor` did `.slice(0, 40).replace(/-+$/, '')`, and stripping a trailing HYPHEN never removes the word STUMP a mid-word cut leaves. Low severity by any functional measure — the ref is valid and everything works — but a branch name is read by a human in `git branch`, in `gh pr list` and in every merge commit for the life of the repo, so the carelessness is permanent and free to avoid. It was noticed by the human as 'no lo veo muy prolijo' before anyone looked at the code, which is the useful part: a cosmetic defect in a name was the first thing a user reacted to about `wst run`, ahead of anything the dispatch actually does. Fixed by cutting at the last word boundary that fits, with a hard cut retained only when the first word alone exceeds the budget (a stump beats an empty branch name). Note also that the RED test I wrote asserted the wrong expected value — I predicted the cut one word earlier than it lands — and the failing test caught my error rather than the code's. Lesson: output a human will live with for years deserves the same care as output a machine parses, and 'it is only cosmetic' is the argument that lets a permanent blemish ship.
